name: Goody Hale

inspiration.original: The witch of the witch-hunt films
inspiration.oldScript: The witch as an evil woman whose power must be burned out.
inspiration.newLens: A healer the town founders erased. Her magic only ever healed; the Best ending marks her grave and tells her real name.

logline: Every October Glimmer Falls burns a straw witch on the roundabout for Founders' Day. This year the briars are growing over the founders' houses, the town's women are sleepwalking into the woods, and the witch has come to watch.
backstory: Temperance Hale came west in 1849 and stayed when the gold ran out, a widow living in a cabin by Crystal Springs with the best herb garden in the foothills. She learned the local plants from Nisenan women who had tended them for thousands of years, and she set bones, broke fevers and delivered more than two hundred babies for miners' wives, Chinese laborers and anyone else who knocked. In 1859 three men decided to build a town on her springs: Josiah Crane, the Reverend Amos Pell and Dr. Lucius Averill, the new doctor who wanted her patients. That summer Crane's daughter Eliza took a fever. Averill bled her four times, and she died. Crane needed someone to blame, and Temperance had sat up with the girl. At a township meeting they named her a witch, voided her land claim and burned her garden while she watched. She died in the woods that winter. The women she had helped buried her in secret under her own garden, which is now the roundabout around the Heartstone, and every Founders' Day since, the town has burned her in effigy.

centralIssue.title: A healer called a witch, and a grave with no name
centralIssue.summary: Temperance Hale healed this valley before it was a town. The founders took her land, burned her garden and branded her a witch to cover their own failure, and she lies under the roundabout with no name while their obelisks stand at Pinecrest. Her healing was never the evil here. Tell the truth, honor her, and give her grave a name.

poster: A tall woman in gray 1850s homespun rising from a suburban roundabout garden at night, a crown of briars and marigolds on her loose gray hair, a lantern burning green in one hand and a stone mortar in the other, thorny vines spiraling over split-level houses, a straw effigy toppled at her feet
portrait: Close portrait of a weathered woman in her late forties with gray-streaked hair falling loose, a crown of briars and orange calendula, deep lines of grief around kind, furious eyes, a sprig of yarrow tucked behind one ear, lit green from below by a lantern
endingPhoto: A tall woman in gray 1850s homespun rising from a suburban roundabout garden at night, a crown of briars and marigolds on her loose gray hair, a lantern burning green in her hand, thorny vines curling over mailboxes and lawn flamingos, a ring of teens joining hands around her with candles
taunts: I sat up with your town's great-great-grandmothers through their fevers. Did they tell you that?
Every year you burn me. Every year I watch.
My garden fed this valley. Your founders salted it.
Names are cheap in Glimmer Falls. They gave me theirs for free: witch.

clues.title: The 1859 register
clues.hint: The founders are buried under obelisks at Pinecrest. The old township ledger and burial register sit in a box in St. Jude's basement.

encounter.title: Founders' Row
encounter.place: Pinecrest Cemetery and St. Jude's basement
encounter.text: Founders' Row has three tall obelisks: CRANE, PELL, AVERILL. Overnight, briars have grown up all three, thick as rope, studded with white roses. A small, plain stone beside the Crane obelisk reads ELIZA, AGED 11, and it is the only one with no thorns on it. Down the hill, the basement door of St. Jude's is propped open, and Father Iggy is carrying out a water-stained box marked UNION CHAPEL 1855-1870.
encounter.art: Three tall granite obelisks in a row on a hillside cemetery wrapped in thick briars as heavy as rope and studded with white roses, a small plain child's headstone beside them clean and bare, a teenager kneeling at the small stone, and down the hill a young priest with a black spiked pompadour and a white collar under a band T-shirt carrying a water-stained cardboard archive box out of a church basement door, overcast morning light, wide shot

choices.label: Help Father Iggy go through the old register

success.text: Page after page of births: Delivered by T. Hale, midwife. Two hundred and twelve times. Then, August 1859: Eliza Crane, fever, attended by Dr. L. Averill, bled four times. Died. Two weeks later, the township minutes: Resolved, that the Widow Hale's claim upon the springs is void, she being of ill repute. Iggy crosses himself. "They needed her land, and they needed somebody to blame."
success.art: A teenager and a punk priest leaning over an old leather register under a basement bulb, a column of births listing one midwife's name again and again

failure.text: The pages are so water-damaged they crumble when you turn them. As the last one flakes away, every briar on Founders' Row tightens with a creak you can hear from the basement, and a white rose petal drifts down the stairs.
failure.art: Crumbling yellowed register pages flaking apart in a teenager's hands in a dim church basement, a single white rose petal drifting down the steps

choices.label: Kneel and clear the moss off Eliza's little headstone

success.text: Under the moss, on the back of the stone, someone has scratched letters with a nail, long ago: MRS. HALE SAT WITH HER THREE NIGHTS. FATHER WOULD NOT LET HER STAY THE FOURTH. Under that, smaller: I AM SORRY. M. CRANE. Eliza's mother knew. She just never said it out loud.
success.art: A teenager kneeling to scrape moss from the back of a small weathered child's headstone, revealing faint scratched letters, briar-wrapped obelisks looming above

failure.text: The moss will not come off. As you scrub, the briars on the Crane obelisk lean down toward you, slowly, almost curious, and a thorn catches your sleeve and holds it. You tear free and leave a strip of flannel behind.
failure.art: A thorny briar from a founder's obelisk leaning down to snag a teenager's flannel sleeve as they kneel at a small headstone

choices.label: Lay out a tarot spread on Founders' Row

success.text: The Empress, reversed. Justice. The Tower. Then the cards blow over in a breeze that smells like yarrow, and they land on the church steps pointing straight at the basement box. Inside: the register, the births, Eliza's death under Dr. Averill's lancet, and the vote that took Temperance's land.
success.art: Tarot cards scattering in a sudden breeze across a cemetery path toward a church basement door, a teenager chasing them past briar-wrapped obelisks

failure.text: Every card you turn is the same card: a woman tied to a stake, a town watching with torches. On the fourth one, the woman in the picture turns her head and looks at you. You put the deck away very carefully.
failure.art: A tarot card on a cemetery path showing a woman at a stake surrounded by a torch-lit crowd, her painted head turned toward the viewer

clues.title: Temperance's receipt book
clues.hint: The occult stacks at the library hold a 1922 book called Witches and Wonders of the Gold Country. It is thicker than it should be.

encounter.title: Witches and Wonders
encounter.place: Occult stacks, Glimmer Falls Public Library
encounter.text: Witches and Wonders of the Gold Country has a lurid cover: a cackling hag over a cauldron, labeled THE WITCH OF CRYSTAL WOODS. Inside, the middle pages have been cut into a hollow, and nested in it is a small leather book tied with faded green ribbon. It smells like lavender and woodsmoke. On the first page, in brown ink: Receipts for the Sick, kept by T. Hale.
encounter.art: A narrow aisle of old library shelves, a lurid 1920s book with a painted cackling hag over a cauldron on its front lying open on a library table, the middle pages cut into a hollow holding a small brown leather notebook tied with faded green ribbon, dried lavender sprigs spilling out, a 16-year-old Indian American girl with a long braid and round gold glasses leaning over it beside a teenager, warm green-shaded lamp light, close medium shot

choices.label: Read the receipt book with Priya in the stacks

success.text: Willow bark for Mrs. O'Day's fever, both twins well. Yarrow and clean linen for Ah Ling's boy's leg, healing. Feverfew for Mr. Pell's headaches, no charge. Priya traces the last entry: "Josiah says the township needs the springs. I told him the land needs no one, only tending. I fear they will make me a story." Priya looks up. "They made her a story."
success.alone: Willow bark for Mrs. O'Day's fever, both twins well. Yarrow and clean linen for Ah Ling's boy's leg, healing. Feverfew for Mr. Pell's headaches, no charge. You trace the last entry with one finger: "Josiah says the township needs the springs. I told him the land needs no one, only tending. I fear they will make me a story." You look up at the lurid cover. They made her a story.
success.art: Two teenagers on the floor of library stacks reading a small leather herbal by lamplight, pressed flowers between the pages, careful handwritten remedies

failure.text: The ink fades as you read, word by word, until the pages are blank. Through the window, the roundabout on Crystal Street is a mile away, but you can see from here that every plant in it has turned to face the library.
failure.art: A small leather notebook whose handwriting fades away on the page, through a library window a distant roundabout garden with every plant turned the same way

choices.label: Take the book to the desk and check it out properly

success.text: The due-date card has been stamped once, in 1923, by M. CRANE. Some Crane descendant read this and hid it inside a book calling her a witch, the one place no one would think to look for the truth. At home you read it cover to cover: remedies, babies, fevers broken, and the founders' threat in her own careful hand.
success.art: A library due-date card stamped once in 1923, slid from the pocket of an old book, a teenager reading a leather herbal at a kitchen table at night

failure.text: The desk computer says the book does not exist. When you turn around to argue, the hollow is empty. You find it two hours later on your own bed at home, open, with a sprig of rue across the page that reads: Not yet.
failure.art: A small leather herbal lying open on a teenager's bedspread at dusk, a sprig of rue laid across the page, the window open to the trees

clues.title: The stone under the Heartstone
clues.hint: Pearl Washington says the same herbs come up in the Heartstone roundabout every spring no matter how many times the HOA sprays it.

encounter.title: The Garden That Comes Back
encounter.text: The HOA plants marigolds in the roundabout every spring, neat in rows. Every spring something else comes up through them: feverfew, yarrow, rue, calendula, in a patch about six feet long and two feet wide, right against the Heartstone's lip. Pearl Washington is out on her porch with her shotgun across her knees and her coffee in her hand, watching you look at it. "Took you kids long enough," she says.
encounter.art: A suburban roundabout garden around a huge purple crystal rock, neat rows of orange marigolds broken by a wild six-foot rectangle of feverfew, yarrow, rue and calendula pressed against the rock's base, a teenager kneeling at the herbs, and on the porch across the street a 71-year-old Black woman in a marigold headwrap and an olive army jacket sitting with a coffee cup and a shotgun across her knees, bright noon sun, wide shot

choices.label: Sit on Pearl's steps and ask what she knows

success.text: "My grandmother grew those same plants in Louisiana for fevers and births. You don't get them in a rectangle by accident." Pearl walks you to the Heartstone and taps a flat river stone wedged under it with her cane. Scratched in it, worn soft: T.H. 1859. SHE HEALED US. "That's a grave, child. Somebody's been tending it for a hundred and twenty-seven years."
success.art: An elderly woman tapping a flat river stone wedged beneath a purple geode with her cane, faint scratched initials and words visible, a teenager crouching beside her among wild herbs

failure.text: Pearl only rocks and sips. "Some things you find for yourself." When you step into the roundabout, the yarrow wraps gently around your ankles and will not let you closer to the stone. It is not angry. It is guarding something.
failure.art: Feathery yarrow stems wrapping gently around a teenager's sneakers in a roundabout garden, holding them back from the base of a purple geode

choices.label: Bring Dr. Haddad to identify the plants

success.text: Dr. Haddad kneels and names them like old friends. "Feverfew, for fever. Yarrow, to stop bleeding. Calendula for wounds, rue for pain. Somebody planted a medicine chest." Under the calendula he brushes away dirt from a river stone: T.H. 1859. SHE HEALED US. He takes off his glasses. "Somebody planted this on a grave."
success.art: A veterinarian kneeling in a roundabout garden naming herbs, brushing soil from a flat river stone with scratched initials, a teenager holding a field guide

failure.text: Dr. Haddad reaches for a calendula and pulls his hand back with a hiss. Every plant in the patch has grown thorns it never had. "These are not supposed to do that," he says, and wraps his thumb in his handkerchief.
failure.art: A veterinarian pulling back a pricked hand from calendula flowers that have suddenly sprouted thorns, a teenager staring at the bristling garden

choices.label: Come back at midnight and brush the leaves from the Heartstone's base

success.text: Your flashlight finds the stone. T.H. 1859. SHE HEALED US. As you read it, the whole patch of herbs breathes out at once, a smell of lavender and woodsmoke, and you hear a woman's voice say, very tired: "Someone finally read it." Nothing else happens. You walk home slowly.
success.art: A flashlight beam on a scratched river stone under a purple geode at midnight, wild herbs swaying in still air, a faint gray figure in homespun at the edge of the light

failure.text: The Heartstone pulses purple, and every porch light on the street goes out. In the dark, the herbs rise up around you to waist height. When the lights come back on, you are standing on the far side of the street with dirt on your hands and no memory of crossing.
failure.art: A dark cul-de-sac with porch lights out, wild herbs rising waist-high around a pulsing purple geode, a teenager standing dazed across the street

signature.title: The Briar Hedge
signature.text: Overnight, briars have swallowed 3 Crystal Street, home of Councilman Hollis Crane, great-great-grandson of the founder. Thorny canes as thick as your wrist wrap the doors, the garage and the satellite dish, blooming with white roses. Upstairs, his daughter Abigail is pounding on her window. Her father is asleep in a chair on the lawn, briars curled gently around his ankles, like a cat.
signature.art: A suburban split-level house at night completely wrapped in thorny briars as thick as a wrist, canes over the doors, the garage and a satellite dish, blooming with white roses, a teenage girl pounding on an upstairs window, a middle-aged man in a cardigan asleep in a lawn chair on the front lawn with briars curled around his ankles, a teenager with a garden spade at the edge of the hedge, white moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Hack a path through the briars to the front door

success.text: Coach Pruitt rips out canes with leather gloves while you chop with a garden spade. You reach the door, kick it in and lead Abigail out. Behind you the briars sigh and slowly grow back, not to trap anyone now, only to hide the house, like a hand over a face.
success.art: A fierce softball coach in leather gloves tearing out thorny canes beside a teenager with a garden spade, leading a girl out of a briar-choked front door

failure.text: Every cane you cut sends up two more. Thorns rake your arms, and when you finally give up, panting, the roses have all turned red. Abigail is still at the window. She has stopped pounding. She is just watching.
failure.art: A scratched, panting teenager surrounded by regrowing briars whose roses have turned blood red, a girl watching silently from an upstairs window

choices.label: Put your hand on the briars and say you know whose garden they came from

success.text: "You were a garden," you tell them. "Somebody burned you." The canes shiver. A path opens, thorns folding back like cats' claws, all the way to the door. As Abigail runs out, a single white rose drops into your hand, thornless.
success.art: A teenager with a hand pressed gently to a wall of briars as the thorny canes fold back to open a path to a front door, a single thornless white rose falling into their palm

failure.text: The briars do not know you. They know only one family name on this street, and tonight it makes them furious. A cane slaps your hand away, hard, and you hear something in the roses whisper: Crane. Crane. Crane.
failure.art: A briar cane lashing a teenager's hand away from a thorny hedge, white roses trembling and whispering in the dark

choices.label: Climb the briars like a trellis to Abigail's window

success.text: You find handholds between the thorns, climb, and pry the window open. Abigail climbs onto your back. She whispers the whole way down: "I keep dreaming about a woman in a gray dress grinding something in a bowl. She isn't scary. She's sad."
success.art: A teenager climbing a briar-covered wall with a girl clinging to their back, moonlight through white roses, a lit window above them

failure.text: Halfway up, the briars shift their grip and hang you upside down by your sneaker. You dangle there, scratched and swearing, until dawn loosens them and dumps you in the rosebushes.
failure.art: A teenager hanging upside down by one sneaker from a briar-wrapped house at night, scratched and furious, white roses all around

signature.title: The Midnight Circle
signature.place: The last stand of Crystal Woods, behind the cul-de-sac
signature.text: Behind the cul-de-sac's back fences, in the last few acres of oak woods the developer never cleared, a circle of women and girls kneels around a green lantern. Their eyes are closed. They are sleepwalking. Abigail Crane is there, and your English teacher, and the PTA treasurer in curlers. Each grinds herbs in a stone mortar and murmurs the same long chant, and the air smells like lavender, woodsmoke and something sharper, like a storm.
signature.art: A moonlit stand of old oak trees behind suburban back fences, a circle of women and girls in nightgowns, robes and hair curlers kneeling with eyes closed around a lantern burning with a green flame, each grinding herbs in a stone mortar, a teenager crouching at the edge of the circle, green lantern light on their faces and blue moonlight through the leaves, wide shot

choices.label: Kneel in the circle and listen to the chant

success.text: It is not a curse. It is a list. Mary O'Day, twins, both well. Ah Ling's boy, leg mended. Sarah Pell, a daughter. Name after name after name, every person Temperance Hale ever healed. Raven squeezes your hand. "She's not casting anything," they whisper. "She's remembering. They took her name, so she keeps everyone else's."
success.alone: It is not a curse. It is a list. Mary O'Day, twins, both well. Ah Ling's boy, leg mended. Sarah Pell, a daughter. Name after name after name, every person Temperance Hale ever healed. Slowly you understand. She's not casting anything. She's remembering. They took her name, so she keeps everyone else's.
success.art: A teenager and a goth tarot reader kneeling side by side in a circle of sleepwalking women, eyes wide as faint glowing names drift up from the stone mortars into the dark

failure.text: The chant gets into your mouth. You find yourself grinding herbs with your bare hands, saying names you have never heard, and under them three new ones, hissed: Crane, Pell, Averill. You come to at dawn with green-stained fingers.
failure.art: A teenager waking at dawn in an oak grove with green-stained fingers and a stone mortar in their lap, the circle of sleepwalkers gone

choices.label: Wake them one at a time, gently, so nobody gets hurt

success.text: You kneel by each woman and say her name softly until she blinks. They wake confused and embarrassed, but every one of them is holding a little cloth packet. Your English teacher sniffs hers. "This is a poultice. My mother made these for my knee." Whatever Goody Hale is doing out here, the medicine is real.
success.art: A teenager gently waking a woman in curlers in a moonlit grove, other women blinking awake holding small cloth herb packets, a green lantern dimming

failure.text: The first one you touch wakes screaming, and then they all do. In the chaos the lantern flares, and a tall shadow in a gray dress stands up behind the circle and turns its face toward you. You do not remember running, but you are home.
failure.art: Sleepwalking women waking up screaming in a grove as a lantern flares green, a tall gray shadow rising behind them

choices.label: Sneak into the middle and snatch the green lantern

success.text: Your fingers close on the handle. It is cold, not hot, and the flame inside is green and steady. The circle sighs and all the sleepers settle onto the moss, peaceful. In the lantern's glow you see an old cabin, a garden, and a woman in gray laughing with a baby in her arms. Then the flame shrinks to a pinprick, and you set it down very gently.
success.art: A teenager holding a cold green lantern in a moonlit grove, its flame revealing a ghostly image of a cabin, an herb garden and a laughing woman holding a baby

failure.text: The lantern is not where it was. It is behind you. It is in a gray hand. A voice says, quiet and tired: "They took everything else. Not this." A gust of cold air pushes you out of the woods and onto the cul-de-sac on your back.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled on their back on a suburban street at night, blown out of the woods, a green lantern glowing between the trees behind them

signature.title: Say It Three Times
signature.place: The upstairs bathroom at Becky Pell's sleepover, 12 Crystal Street, midnight
signature.text: Becky Pell's sleepover has reached the dare portion of the night. The whole party, in sleeping bags and face masks, has shoved you into the upstairs bathroom with a lit candle, the light off, and one rule: look in the mirror and say "Goody Hale" three times. Becky's great-great-great-grandfather was a town founder, and she thinks this is hilarious. You have said it twice. The mirror has fogged over on its own, and behind your reflection, where the shower curtain should be, there is a garden at night.
signature.art: A dark upstairs bathroom at midnight, a teenager holding a lit candle in front of a fogged mirror, and in the mirror behind their reflection, where the shower curtain should be, a moonlit garden of herbs drying on strings with a tall gray-haired woman standing among the rows, giggling teens in sleeping bags and green face masks crowded in the doorway behind, candle flame and blue mirror light, medium shot

choices.label: Say it the third time, and mean it

success.text: "Goody Hale." The fog clears onto a summer garden, rows of herbs drying on strings, and a tall woman in gray looks up from her work, startled, as if nobody has called her anything in a very long time. She tilts her head at you. When the candle gutters, there is a sprig of lavender lying on the sink.
success.art: A teenager with a candle before a bathroom mirror showing a sunlit herb garden with bundles drying on strings, a tall woman in gray homespun looking up startled, a sprig of lavender lying on the sink

failure.text: On the third name the candle goes out and the mirror cracks into a web of thorny lines, like briars. Everyone outside the door screams, Mrs. Pell storms upstairs in her bathrobe, and somehow you are the one who has to explain the mirror.
failure.art: A bathroom mirror cracked into a web of briar-shaped lines around a teenager's startled reflection, a smoking snuffed candle, a furious mother in a bathrobe filling the doorway behind

choices.label: Talk to her like a neighbor: "Mrs. Hale, are you all right?"

success.text: The fog in the mirror goes warm, like breath. A tired voice answers from somewhere past the glass: "Nobody's asked me that in a hundred years." When the light comes back on, a small cloth packet tied with string sits on the sink, smelling of mint and chamomile. It works on headaches better than anything in the medicine cabinet.
success.art: A teenager speaking gently to a softly glowing fogged bathroom mirror, the faint outline of a tired woman in gray beyond the glass, a small string-tied cloth herb packet resting on the sink

failure.text: The voice past the glass laughs, short and bitter. "Manners. The men who burned my garden had lovely manners." The fog freezes into frost ferns across the mirror, and outside the door Becky's whole sleepover screams at once.
failure.art: A bathroom mirror frosted over with icy fern patterns around a teenager's shocked reflection, a candle flame bent sideways by a cold draft, sleeping bags visible through the doorway

choices.label: Blow out the candle and flip on the light before anything happens

success.text: You hit the switch, the hamper beside the tub explodes, and a black cat rockets out of it and through everyone's legs. The whole sleepover screams, then laughs until they cry. The cat belongs to Becky's little brother. The mirror is just a mirror. Probably.
success.art: A black cat launching out of a wicker laundry hamper in a brightly lit bathroom, a teenager by the light switch, pajama-clad teens in the doorway shrieking and laughing

failure.text: The switch clicks and the room stays dark. The candle is still burning, though you blew it out. In the mirror, a black cat sits on the sink, watching you. In the room, the sink is empty.
failure.art: A teenager frozen beside a bathroom light switch in candlelight, a mirror reflecting a black cat sitting calmly on the sink, the real sink in the room bare and gleaming

signature.title: Dunk the Witch
signature.place: The Founders' Day carnival lot behind St. Jude's, eleven p.m.
signature.text: The Founders' Day committee set up its carnival a day early, and the star attraction is a dunk tank painted with a cackling green witch: DUNK THE WITCH, THREE BALLS FOR A QUARTER. Nobody is running it tonight, but it is running anyway. Hannah Averill from your homeroom sits on the plank in a pointed hat, sleepwalking, eyes closed, while softballs rise one by one out of a bucket and hang in the air, aiming at the target.
signature.art: A carnival dunk tank on a dark church parking lot at eleven at night, painted with a cackling green-faced witch, a sleepwalking teenage girl in a black pointed hat sitting on the plank above the water with her eyes closed, three softballs hanging in midair aimed at the round target, a bucket of balls tipped over, a teenager running toward the chicken-wire cage, string bulbs and dark sky, wide shot

choices.label: Vault the cage and pull Hannah off the plank

success.text: You go over the chicken wire and haul Hannah off the plank just as a softball smacks the target. The seat drops into the tank with a splash like a gasp. Hannah wakes up in your arms, shivering. "I dreamed the whole town was watching," she whispers, "and laughing, and none of them would help."
success.art: A teenager hauling a sleepwalking girl in a pointed hat off the plank of a carnival dunk tank at night, the seat dropping into a splash, softballs hanging in the air

failure.text: You are one second late. The ball hits and you both go in. The water is black and ice-cold and tastes of woodsmoke, and for one long moment it holds you under. You surface gasping, Hannah coughing beside you, awake and furious and scared.
failure.art: Two soaked teens bursting up out of the dark water of a carnival dunk tank at night, gasping, a pointed witch hat floating beside them, softballs bobbing on the surface

choices.label: Jam the target arm with a bat before the next throw

success.text: You ram the bat through the target bracket and wedge it tight. The next ball clanks, and clanks again, and the seat stays put. One by one the softballs drop to the grass like windfall apples, and Hannah sleepwalks off the plank and home to bed without ever knowing. You keep the quarters from the cash box for your trouble.
success.art: A baseball bat jammed through the target arm of a carnival dunk tank at night, softballs dropping into the grass like apples, a sleepwalking girl in a pointed hat wandering away toward the street

failure.text: The bat snaps clean in half. The next ball hits, the seat drops, and while you are fishing Hannah out of the tank, every softball left in the bucket rises and turns toward you.
failure.art: A teenager fishing a sleepwalking girl out of a dunk tank at night, a snapped baseball bat on the grass, a dozen softballs rising from a bucket and turning toward them

choices.label: Tell the tank the truth: the old witch test was always rigged

success.text: "Float and you're a witch. Sink and you're innocent," you say out loud. "Nobody could ever win." The floating softballs drop all at once into the grass. On the surface of the tank, for a moment, a tall woman in gray nods at you, and the green witch painted on the side fades to a pale smudge.
success.art: A teenager speaking to the dark still water of a carnival dunk tank at night, softballs dropping into the grass, the faint reflection of a tall woman in gray nodding on the surface

failure.text: The water hears a lecture, not an apology. It heaves over the glass in one cold wave and soaks you to the skin, and when you wipe your eyes, someone has jammed the pointed hat on your head. The softballs go right on floating.
failure.art: A drenched teenager wearing a soggy pointed witch hat beside a carnival dunk tank sloshing over at night, softballs still floating in midair around them

signature.title: The Poppets
signature.place: The porches of Crystal Street, one a.m.
signature.text: Overnight, little muslin dolls have appeared on Crystal Street, each one stuffed with herbs and tied by a red ribbon to a porch light: on the Crane house, the Pell house, the Averill house, and, for some reason, yours. Now a flashlight patrol of Founders' Day committee members in bathrobes is going door to door, led by Mrs. Dolores Pell, stuffing the dolls into a trash bag. "Devil work," she announces. In the roundabout, a garbage can is already burning.
signature.art: Small muslin dolls stuffed with herbs tied by red ribbons to the porch lights of suburban houses at one in the morning, a patrol of neighbors in bathrobes with flashlights led by a stern woman stuffing the dolls into a black trash bag, a metal garbage can burning on the roundabout down the street, a teenager on their porch holding one doll, yellow porch lights and orange fire glow, wide shot

choices.label: Open your poppet and see what is really inside

success.text: You slit the seam and find feverfew, chamomile, peppermint and willow bark. "That's a fever remedy," you tell the patrol. "Whoever made these is trying to keep you well." Mrs. Pell sniffs one, and her face crumples like a girl's: her own grandmother used to tuck these under pillows.
success.art: A teenager on a suburban porch at night opening a small muslin doll to reveal dried flowers and herbs, a woman in a bathrobe with a flashlight leaning in to sniff, a red ribbon dangling from a porch light

failure.text: The herbs puff into your face and you sneeze five times in a row, enormous honking sneezes. The patrol decides you are in on it and chases you off the porch with flashlights, and someone drops your poppet into the bag.
failure.art: A sneezing teenager fleeing a porch at night pursued by neighbors in bathrobes waving flashlights, a cloud of dried herbs in the air, a muslin doll dropping into a trash bag

choices.label: Stand between the patrol and the burning can

success.text: You plant yourself in front of the burning can with your arms out. Father Iggy, bass case still on his back from band practice, walks up beside you, takes a poppet from the bag, blesses it and hangs it back on the nearest porch. "Nobody burns anybody's medicine tonight," he says mildly. The patrol drifts home, grumbling, and the fire burns itself out.
success.alone: You plant yourself in front of the burning can with your arms out. Then you take a poppet from the bag and hang it back on the nearest porch. "Nobody burns anybody's medicine tonight," you say, as mildly as you can. The patrol drifts home, grumbling, and the fire burns itself out.
success.art: A teenager standing with arms spread before a burning garbage can on a suburban roundabout at night, a young priest with a bass guitar case on his back hanging a muslin doll on a porch light, neighbors in bathrobes retreating

failure.text: Someone shoulders past you and dumps the bag into the can. The fire flares up green, the whole street fills with the smell of burning lavender, and far off in the oak woods behind the back fences, a woman begins to cry.
failure.art: A garbage can fire flaring bright green on a suburban roundabout at night, a trash bag of muslin dolls tumbling into the flames, smoke curling toward dark oak woods behind backyard fences

choices.label: Steal the bag back and rehang every poppet before dawn

success.text: While the patrol argues over the fire, you slip the bag off Mrs. Pell's porch rail and spend until dawn creeping house to house, tying red ribbons back onto porch lights. In the morning, the briars pushing up through the founders' lawns stop at the bottom step of every house with a poppet, as if someone asked them nicely to wait.
success.art: A teenager on tiptoe tying a red-ribboned muslin doll back onto a porch light at dawn, a trash bag over one shoulder, thorny briars curling up through the lawn and stopping at the bottom step

failure.text: Mrs. Pell catches you by the hood halfway down her steps and marches you home in front of the whole street, announcing to every porch that she has caught the culprit. The poppets go in the fire anyway.
failure.art: A stern woman in a bathrobe and curlers marching a teenager by the hood down a suburban sidewalk at night, neighbors watching from lit porches, a garbage can fire glowing in the roundabout

signature.title: The Effigy
signature.text: The Founders' Day committee has built tomorrow's effigy: a straw witch with a pointed hat, a green paper face and a sign around its neck that says BEGONE, tied to a stake in the roundabout. At midnight you find a woman standing beside it, tall and gray, in homespun with her hair loose. She is touching its straw cheek. All down Crystal Street, briars are bursting up through the lawns of every house that a founder's family still owns, and crows are landing on every roof.
signature.art: A straw witch effigy with a black pointed hat and a green paper face tied to a wooden stake on a suburban roundabout at midnight, a cardboard square hung on its chest, a tall weathered woman in gray 1850s homespun with long loose gray-streaked hair touching its straw cheek, thick briars bursting up through nearby lawns, crows lining every rooftop, a teenager standing a few steps behind her, white moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Walk up and tell her you know they lied

success.text: She does not turn around. "One hundred and twenty-seven years they've burned me," Temperance says. "Children cheer. I delivered their great-grandparents." Then she looks at you, and her eyes are not cruel at all, only exhausted. "If you know, then say it tomorrow. Out loud. In front of all of them." The crows lift off the roofs at once.
success.art: A tall gray woman in homespun turning from a straw effigy to face a teenager on a roundabout at midnight, her eyes weary and kind, a cloud of crows lifting off the rooftops

failure.text: She turns and looks through you as if you were one more face in the crowd with a torch. "They all say they're different," she says. The briars along the street surge a foot higher, and the crows begin, all together, to scream.
failure.art: A gray ghostly woman looking past a teenager on a dark roundabout, briars surging up along the street, crows screaming from every roof

choices.label: Cut the effigy down and hide it in Wade's van

success.text: You saw through the ropes, Wade backs the van onto the curb with the lights off, and the straw witch goes in the back under a pile of jackets. The gray woman watches you do it. She does not stop you. When you look again, she is gone, and the briars on the nearest lawn have stopped growing.
success.alone: You saw through the ropes and stuff the straw witch into the back of the van parked on the curb, under a pile of jackets. The gray woman watches you do it. She does not stop you. When you look again, she is gone, and the briars on the nearest lawn have stopped growing.
success.art: Two teens loading a straw witch effigy into the back of a battered metalhead's van at midnight, a gray ghostly woman watching silently from the roundabout

failure.text: Halfway through the ropes, porch lights snap on. The committee chairman is in his bathrobe on the curb shouting about vandals, and the effigy stays up. Behind him, a briar is climbing his porch post, faster now.
failure.art: A committee chairman in a bathrobe shouting from the curb at teens caught sawing at an effigy's ropes, a briar racing up his porch post behind him

choices.label: Light up the roundabout and stand your ground against the crows

success.text: The crows dive, and you hold your flashlight high and do not run. They pull up at the last second, wheel around the Heartstone and settle on the roundabout curb in a ring, watching you with bright, considering eyes. Something has noticed that you stayed.
success.art: A teenager holding a flashlight high on a roundabout as a flock of crows pulls up from a dive and settles in a ring on the curb around them

failure.text: The crows come down in a black storm of wings and you go flat on the grass with your arms over your head. When they lift, your flashlight is gone and so is the gray woman, and the effigy's paper face is smiling now.
failure.art: A teenager flat on a roundabout lawn under a storm of crow wings, a straw effigy above them with its paper face now smiling

signature.title: Apples on the Doorstep
signature.place: The porches of Crystal Street, eleven p.m.
signature.text: It is 1986, the year every parent in Glimmer Falls inspects Halloween candy like a bomb squad, and tonight a woven basket of shining red apples has appeared on every porch on Crystal Street. They are a small, striped, old-fashioned kind that nobody has grown in this valley for a hundred years. Mrs. Dolores Pell is already going door to door in her bathrobe with a flashlight, stuffing them into a garbage bag and announcing that they are poisoned. Your basket is still sitting on your welcome mat, smelling like late summer.
signature.art: A woven basket of small striped red heirloom apples sitting on a suburban welcome mat at eleven at night, shining under a warm gold porch light, a teenager crouching beside it holding one apple, and across the street a woman in a bathrobe with a flashlight and a black garbage bag marching up the next driveway, warm porch light and blue night, medium shot

choices.label: Take a bite, right there on the porch

success.text: It is crisp and tart and tastes like a summer afternoon a long time ago. For one second you see an orchard where the roundabout stands, and a tall woman in gray on a ladder, tossing apples down to children. The ache of the whole week drains out of your shoulders, and you sleep like a stone.
success.art: A teenager biting a striped red apple on a porch at night, a dreamy vision of a sunlit orchard shimmering around them, a tall woman in a gray homespun dress on a wooden ladder tossing apples to laughing children

failure.text: The apple is perfectly fine. You, unfortunately, bite it at the exact moment Mrs. Pell's flashlight finds you, and she screams so loudly the whole street comes out to watch you get marched home "for observation." You lie awake all night, healthy and thoroughly embarrassed.
failure.art: A woman in a bathrobe shrieking and pointing a flashlight at a teenager mid-bite on a porch at night, neighbors in robes peering from doorways, a basket of red apples spilling across the steps

choices.label: Take an apple to Dr. Haddad's garage clinic and X-ray it

success.text: Dr. Haddad, in a bathrobe over his scrubs, slides the apple under his clinic's old X-ray machine, the same way the hospital is screening candy bars this week. The film shows exactly what an apple should hold: seeds, set in a perfect five-pointed star. "This is an old variety," he says, turning it in his hand. "Somebody here grew these once."
success.art: A veterinarian in a bathrobe over scrubs holding an X-ray film to a light box in a cluttered garage clinic at night, the film showing apple seeds in a star, a curious teenager and a three-legged cat beside him

failure.text: The X-ray machine coughs and blacks out the whole garage, and Dr. Haddad's three-legged cat knocks the apple into a bin of rubber gloves. By the time you find it, Mrs. Pell's patrol has collected every basket on the street and is carrying them to the burning can.
failure.art: A dark garage clinic lit by a single sparking X-ray machine, a three-legged cat leaping off a counter, a teenager digging through a bin of rubber gloves, flashlights bobbing outside the window

choices.label: Bake the apples into a pie and bring a slice to Mrs. Pell

success.text: You bake until two in the morning and carry a slice across the street on your best plate. Mrs. Pell eyes it, sniffs it, takes one bite, and her face goes soft and young. "My grandmother made pie with apples just like these," she says quietly, "from a tree behind the church that the town cut down." She sets the garbage bag on the porch and does not pick it up again.
success.art: A teenager offering a warm slice of apple pie on a china plate to a woman in a bathrobe on her porch at night, her face softening as she takes a bite, a garbage bag of apples slumped beside her slippers

failure.text: The pie comes out black on top and raw in the middle, and when you open the kitchen window to clear the smoke, every crow on the street lands on your sill. Mrs. Pell sees the crows and adds your house to her list.
failure.art: A smoky suburban kitchen at night with a burnt pie on the counter, a row of glossy black crows crowding the open window sill, a teenager waving a dish towel, a flashlight peering in from across the street

signature.title: The Founders' Day Pageant
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls High auditorium, dress rehearsal, 11 p.m.
signature.text: Your history class got roped into the Founders' Day pageant, and the drama teacher has cast you, without asking, as the Witch. The script is the founders' version: a wicked woman, three brave men, a township meeting and a happy town. At the late dress rehearsal, the cardboard meetinghouse starts to smell of real woodsmoke, the actors' fake beards grow in thick and gray, and the boy playing Reverend Pell points at you with a hand that is not his own. "Speak, witch," he says, in a voice from 1859. Out in the dark seats, the parents who came to pick up their kids have all gone very still.
signature.art: A high school auditorium stage at eleven at night dressed as a cardboard 1859 meetinghouse, three teen actors in thick real-looking gray beards and black hats pointing at a teenager in a black pointed witch hat and a green rubber nose, wisps of woodsmoke curling from the painted backdrop, parents sitting perfectly still in the dark seats, hot white stage light, wide shot from the house

choices.label: Answer for her: say what she actually did that summer

success.text: "I sat up with Eliza for three nights," you hear yourself say, and you mean every word. "Willow bark, cool cloths, broth by the spoonful, and the fever was turning when they sent me away." The beards fall off the actors like dead leaves, and a mother in the third row stands up and says, "Let the kid talk." Nobody in that auditorium forgets it.
success.art: A teenager in a witch costume speaking out boldly center stage, fake gray beards drifting off three startled teen actors like leaves, a mother rising from her seat in the dark auditorium

failure.text: Your voice comes out thin and shaking, and the meetinghouse answers with a gavel crack that shakes dust from the rafters. "Guilty," the three founders say together, the parents in the seats murmur along, and the stage lights go out on you standing alone in a pointed hat.
failure.art: A lone teenager in a pointed witch hat in a fading spotlight on a high school stage, three bearded figures with a raised gavel, dust falling from the rafters, murmuring parents in shadow

choices.label: Throw away the green nose and play the Witch as the hero of the show

success.text: You fling the green rubber nose into the orchestra pit and play her like a leading lady: a midwife with a bag of herbs, a sharp tongue and two hundred babies to her name. Glory slips in from the wings with a lantern and starts feeding you better lines. By the end of the scene the parents are cheering, and the founders' beards have wilted into crepe hair.
success.alone: You fling the green rubber nose into the orchestra pit and play her like a leading lady: a midwife with a bag of herbs, a sharp tongue and two hundred babies to her name. You ditch the script and improvise better lines on the fly. By the end of the scene the parents are cheering, and the founders' beards have wilted into crepe hair.
success.art: A teenager striding center stage as a proud frontier midwife with an herb satchel, a drag queen in sequins holding a lantern in the wings, cheering parents, wilted crepe beards on three teen actors

failure.text: The audience laughs, but in the wrong places, the way people laugh at the witch in a school play. The cardboard meetinghouse leans in over you, and the green rubber nose stays stuck until you scrub it off at home with dish soap.
failure.art: A teenager in a green rubber witch nose on a high school stage, a cardboard meetinghouse leaning over them, an audience laughing in the dark, a crooked pointed hat

choices.label: Demand that the prosecution show its evidence

success.text: "Objection," you say. "What exactly is the evidence?" The boy playing Josiah Crane flips through his script, and the pages are blank, and so are the Reverend's, and even the gavel turns out to be cardboard. With nothing behind it, the 1859 meeting fades back into a high school rehearsal, and the drama teacher looks at the script for the first time like he is actually reading it.
success.art: A teenager in a witch costume raising a hand in objection on a high school stage, a bearded teen actor flipping through blank script pages, a cardboard gavel, a drama teacher frowning at a binder in the aisle

failure.text: The founders produce their evidence: a grieving father, a burned garden, a frightened town. None of it proves a thing, but the parents in the dark seats nod anyway, and you are hustled off the stage with a pointed hat jammed down over your ears.
failure.art: Three bearded figures in black hats looming on a high school stage, a teenager hustled offstage with a pointed hat jammed over their ears, parents nodding in the dark auditorium

signature.title: The Torchlight Walk
signature.place: Crystal Street to the old spring, October 30, midnight
signature.text: Every year on the night before Founders' Day, Glimmer Falls holds its Torchlight Walk from the roundabout to the old spring in Crystal Woods, to "drive the witch out of the valley." This year the committee has handed out real torches, and nearly the whole town has come, in parkas and Halloween costumes, flames bobbing down the cul-de-sac. At the edge of the woods the briars have risen into a wall taller than a house, and behind it the sleepwalking women of the circle kneel in a ring. Somebody near the front starts shouting about fire.
signature.art: A long procession of townspeople in parkas and Halloween costumes carrying flaming torches down a suburban street at midnight toward a towering wall of thorny briars blooming with white roses at the edge of dark oak woods, sleepwalking women kneeling in a ring beyond the briars, a teenager standing on a trailhead bench with arms raised, orange torchlight and black woods, wide shot

choices.label: Climb onto the trailhead bench and tell the walkers who really lived at the spring

success.text: You climb onto the bench and tell them: a widow lived at this spring before there was a town, and she delivered more than two hundred of their great-grandparents. A woman in a parka near the front says, "My great-grandmother was one of them. There's a story in our family." Then a man says it, and another, and one by one the torches go down into the wet grass, hissing out.
success.art: A teenager standing on a wooden trailhead bench speaking to a crowd at night, townspeople in parkas lowering their torches into wet grass in curls of smoke, a wall of briars glowing softly behind them

failure.text: The walkers cannot hear you over the committee's bullhorn. The torches surge past your bench toward the briars, the wall of thorns bristles and leans out to meet them, and you spend the rest of the night running buckets from the creek with the few neighbors who believed you.
failure.art: A torchlit crowd surging past a teenager on a trailhead bench toward a bristling wall of briars at night, a man with a bullhorn at the front, a few neighbors hauling buckets of creek water

choices.label: Swap the route markers and lead the walk in circles around the cul-de-sac

success.text: Kev knows every path in Glimmer Falls, and the two of you run ahead swapping the committee's little reflector arrows. The Torchlight Walk marches confidently around the roundabout once, twice, five times, until the torches burn low, the bullhorn goes hoarse and everybody goes home grumbling about bad planning. The briars never see a flame.
success.alone: You know enough shortcuts in Glimmer Falls to run ahead swapping the committee's little reflector arrows. The Torchlight Walk marches confidently around the roundabout once, twice, five times, until the torches burn low, the bullhorn goes hoarse and everybody goes home grumbling about bad planning. The briars never see a flame.
success.art: Two teens sprinting through suburban hedges at night carrying armfuls of reflector arrows, a torchlit procession circling a glowing purple geode roundabout behind them, torches burning low

failure.text: The committee chairman catches you with an armful of arrows and announces it over the bullhorn. Now the whole Torchlight Walk follows you, very slowly, all the way to your house, and the briars on your own lawn burst up a foot higher behind the crowd.
failure.art: A teenager clutching reflector arrows caught in a man's flashlight and bullhorn at night, a torchlit crowd trailing them up a suburban driveway, thorny briars bursting from the front lawn

choices.label: Hijack the walk with a boombox and turn it into a Halloween parade

success.text: You hoist a boombox on your shoulder, crank the mixtape and start a conga line at the front of the walk. Costumed kids join first, then their parents, then half the street, kicking their knees up, and somehow the torches end up stuck in a pumpkin patch like birthday candles. At the edge of the woods, the briar wall sways along to the music and reaches for nobody.
success.art: A joyful conga line of townspeople in Halloween costumes dancing behind a teenager with a boombox on their shoulder at night, torches planted in a pumpkin patch like birthday candles, a briar wall swaying in the background

failure.text: The batteries die halfway through the first song. In the sudden silence the committee's bullhorn takes up the old chant, and your conga line becomes the front of the march, carrying torches right up to the thorns.
failure.art: A teenager with a silent boombox at the head of a torchlit march at night, costumed townspeople pressing forward, a towering wall of thorns looming ahead, a bullhorn raised in the crowd

finale.title: The Burning Garden
finale.text: On Halloween night the Founders' Day bonfire never gets lit. Briars burst from the roundabout and weave a thorn cathedral around the Heartstone, caging Councilman Crane, the committee and every founder's descendant on the street. The sleepwalking women kneel in a ring outside it, grinding herbs. And from the earth of her own garden rises Temperance Hale, crowned with briars and calendula, lantern burning green. "They burned my garden and called it God's work," she says. "They took my land and my name. Tonight, I take theirs."
finale.art: A towering cathedral of woven thorny briars around a glowing purple crystal rock on a suburban roundabout on Halloween night, a councilman in a suit and townspeople caged inside, sleepwalking women in nightgowns kneeling in a ring outside, and rising from the herb garden a tall weathered woman in gray 1850s homespun with loose gray-streaked hair and a crown of briars and orange calendula holding a lantern burning green, four teenagers in homemade costumes facing her, green and violet light, wide shot

choices.label: Hack through the thorn cathedral and pull everyone out

success.text: You tear the briars apart cane by cane and drag the councilman and the committee out through the gap, scratched and sobbing. The cathedral collapses. Temperance looks at you once, without anger, only disappointment, and sinks back into her garden. The grave is quiet. It is still nameless.
success.art: A teen tearing a gap in a thorn cathedral and pulling scratched townspeople free, a gray woman sinking back into a garden with a disappointed look

failure.text: The briars close faster than you can cut. A cane wraps your wrist, gently but completely, and draws you inside the cathedral with the founders' families. You were never her enemy. You were just in the way.
failure.art: A briar cane wrapping a teen's wrist and drawing them into a thorn cathedral among frightened townspeople

choices.label: Rig the floodlights for a false dawn

success.text: Frankie hotwires the Founders' Day floodlights to every porch light on the street and throws the switch. It looks like sunrise. Temperance flinches, the briars wilt, and the women in the ring sink into ordinary sleep. She fades with the false dawn, and her lantern goes out with a sigh. She will sleep. She will not rest.
success.alone: Following the diagram taped inside the junction box, you hotwire the Founders' Day floodlights to every porch light on the street and throw the switch. It looks like sunrise. Temperance flinches, the briars wilt, and the women in the ring sink into ordinary sleep. She fades with the false dawn, and her lantern goes out with a sigh. She will sleep. She will not rest.
success.art: A trans stage manager in a headset throwing a giant switch as floodlights and porch lights blaze like sunrise over a roundabout, a gray woman fading and briars wilting

failure.text: The floodlights blow in a shower of sparks. In the real dark, Temperance's lantern is the only light left, and every face on Crystal Street turns toward it.
failure.art: Floodlights bursting in a shower of sparks over a dark roundabout, a single green lantern glowing as faces turn toward it

choices.label: Read the truth out loud, say the names she saved, and promise her a stone

success.text: You read the register: Eliza Crane, attended by Dr. Averill, bled four times. You read the township vote that stole her land. You read from her receipt book, and the women in the ring wake and say the names with you: Mary O'Day, Ah Ling's boy, Sarah Pell. Then Hollis Crane steps up to the thorns and says, voice shaking, "My family lied about you. I'm sorry. You'll have your name." Temperance lowers the lantern. The briars burst into calendula and feverfew, the cathedral opens like a gate, and for the first time in a hundred and twenty-seven years, the healer of Crystal Springs smiles.
success.art: A teenager reading aloud from an old register beside a weeping councilman at a wall of briars bursting into orange calendula and white feverfew, waking women holding herb packets, a gray woman lowering her green lantern and smiling

failure.text: Your voice is lost in the wind and the crows. Temperance has heard apologies before, from men who went home and changed nothing. The thorns hold. You have the truth. Make her believe someone will act on it.
failure.art: A teenager shouting from a register into a storm of crows and wind before a wall of thorns, a gray woman turning her face away

choices.label: Speak to the thorns as her garden, the way you learned to on the first nights

success.text: On the first nights you learned these briars were a garden before they were a weapon. You lay your palm on the thorn cathedral and tell them, "You were medicine. Let them out, and nobody burns you again." The canes unknot one by one into a doorway, and the founders' families crawl out into the night, while Temperance lowers her lantern and sinks back into her soil to sleep.
success.art: A teenager with a palm pressed to a cathedral of thorny briars at night, the canes unknotting into an arched doorway, frightened families crawling out, a tall woman in gray with a green lantern sinking into the earth

failure.text: The briars remember you, but they remember the Cranes better, and tonight the Cranes are inside. The canes shiver and hold fast. They nearly listened; say it like you mean it.
failure.art: A teenager's hand on a shivering wall of briars at night, thorns tightening, faces of trapped families visible through the canes, a green lantern glowing beyond

choices.label: Plant yourself between the thorns and the town, the way you stood up when the town turned on her

success.text: The town has already watched you stand up for her once. You do it again in front of everyone: you kick the bonfire wood away from the thorns, push the committee back from their matches, then put your shoulder into the briars and haul the founders' families out through the gap. Temperance watches you protect both sides at once, and the cathedral sags and sinks back into the soil.
success.art: A teenager shoving bonfire logs away from a cathedral of briars at night while dragging trapped families through a gap in the thorns, a crowd held back behind them, a tall woman in gray watching with a green lantern

failure.text: You shove, and the thorns shove back harder while the committee shouts over you about devil work. You end up scratched and breathless on the curb. You know how to stand in the middle; plant your feet.
failure.art: A scratched teenager sitting breathless on a curb at night, a wall of briars surging behind them, a committee of townspeople in bathrobes shouting with flashlights

choices.label: Tell the whole town her name, the way you protected her the night before Halloween

success.text: The neighbors who stood with you the night before step up beside you at the thorns. You read the register and her receipt book aloud, and the whole crowd says her name with you: Temperance Hale, midwife and healer. Hollis Crane steps up, voice shaking, and promises her a stone. The briars burst into calendula and feverfew, the cathedral opens like a gate, and the healer of Crystal Springs finally smiles.
success.art: A crowd of townspeople speaking together before a cathedral of briars bursting into orange calendula and white feverfew at night, a teenager reading from an old ledger, a tall woman in gray crowned with flowers smiling, green lantern lowered

failure.text: The crowd's voices falter on her name, and Temperance has heard half-hearted apologies before. The thorns hold. Hold the truth up higher, and give the town a moment to catch up with you.
failure.art: A hesitant crowd murmuring before a wall of thorns at night, a teenager holding up an old ledger, a tall woman in gray with a green lantern watching with tired eyes

best.title: Here Lies Temperance Hale
best.text: In November the town council votes, on Councilman Crane's own motion, to set a granite marker in the roundabout: TEMPERANCE HALE, 1811-1859, MIDWIFE AND HEALER. SHE TENDED THIS VALLEY. The effigy is retired for good, and the Glitter Box rewrites the Founders' Day pageant with Glory as Temperance, receiving a standing ovation from half the town. The HOA stops spraying the herbs. Pearl and Dr. Haddad tend them now, and whenever someone on Crystal Street has a fever, a sprig of feverfew appears on their pillow.
best.art: A new granite marker set among thriving herbs in a suburban roundabout beside a purple crystal rock, a 71-year-old Black woman in a marigold headwrap and a mustached man in a white lab coat kneeling to tend the feverfew and calendula, a tall drag queen in gray 1850s homespun laying a bouquet at the marker, neighbors and teenagers gathered around applauding, bright autumn morning light, wide shot

good.title: Back to Sleep
good.text: The briars die back, the women stop sleepwalking, and the crows leave Crystal Street. Goody Hale sleeps under her garden again. But nobody carves her name, and next October the committee builds a brand-new straw witch with a pointed hat. You do not go to the bonfire. You leave a handful of calendula on the river stone instead.
good.art: A teenager kneeling to leave a handful of orange calendula flowers on a scratched river stone at the base of a purple crystal rock on a roundabout at dusk, and in the distance two men building a new straw figure with a pointed hat on a stake, long golden shadows, medium wide shot

bittersweet.title: Thorns That Stay
bittersweet.text: Everyone gets out of the thorn cathedral, but the briars never leave the Crane house, and the Cranes move away by spring. Women all over Glimmer Falls wake some mornings with dirt under their nails and names on their lips they do not know. Temperance sleeps, but not easily, and neither do you.
bittersweet.art: A suburban split-level house still wrapped in thorny briars and white roses with a moving truck parked at the curb and movers carrying boxes, and in the foreground through a kitchen window across the street a woman at the sink staring at dark soil under her fingernails, gray spring morning light, wide shot

bad.title: Another Name for the List
bad.text: On November first you do not come home. Your crew finds you in the last stand of Crystal Woods, kneeling in the sleepwalkers' ring with your eyes closed, grinding herbs in a stone mortar and murmuring an endless list of names and grudges. Every night you go back. Every night the list gets longer, and the grave stays nameless.
bad.art: A teenager kneeling with closed eyes in a moonlit oak grove grinding herbs in a stone mortar among sleepwalking women in nightgowns around a green lantern, three worried friends watching from behind a wooden back fence with flashlights, green lantern light and white moonlight, wide shot
